analysis.title: Dems At 94% For The House, Trump Vows To "Veto Everything": Here's What Wall Street Expects After Tuesday's Midterms
key_insights: Prediction markets price Democrats at 94% (Polymarket) and 90.7% (Kalshi) to win the House. The Senate, where Republicans hold 53-47, is priced at 68% for Democrats. Every bank cited expects divided government.

Crédit Agricole puts Trump's approval below 40%, more than 20 points underwater. He is 32.4 points underwater on the economy and 43.8 on inflation. The generic ballot favors Democrats by more than 8 points. Republicans hold the House 220-215, so Democrats need a net gain of 3 seats.

Crédit Agricole's outcome odds are Democratic sweep 65%, Democratic House with Republican Senate 25%, Republican sweep 10%. Republican House with Democratic Senate is called highly unlikely. Redistricting limits truly competitive seats to the 20s, so a 40-seat wave is unlikely.
Senate races: Cooper leads by 10.6 in North Carolina, Brown by 3.3 in Ohio, and Talarico by 1.5 over Paxton in Texas. Democrats need a net 4 seats, with Vance breaking a 50-50 tie.

JPMorgan Market Intel shows late moves since last Friday. Kansas went from Democrats +0.4 to even in DDHQ, Maine's Polymarket odds fell from 67% to 62%, Texas rose from 64% to 69%, and Kalshi's Senate control odds fell from 67% to 64%. JPM cites Nate Silver that midterm polling error was zero in 2018 and polls underestimated Democrats in 2022.

Crédit Agricole expects legislative gridlock if Democrats win the House, whatever the Senate result, because of the filibuster and the presidential veto. Trump said he would veto everything a Democratic Congress sends him. The Senate result mainly matters for judicial and other appointments, plus investigations. Crédit Agricole sees a decent chance of another shutdown next year. Tariff and foreign policy would change little.

Citi flags two fiscal deadlines: the December 11 funding deadline, which the lame-duck Congress will probably clear, and the debt ceiling, whose hard date falls around Q4 2027. Citi does not expect a party-line reconciliation bill to raise the limit before the new Congress is seated. It expects deals to go down to the wire and possibly involve slightly looser fiscal policy.

Citi's bottom line is that the deficit stays near 6% of GDP regardless of the election outcome. The FY2026 deficit was $1.99 trillion, with spending up 6% to $7.4 trillion and revenue up 3% to $5.4 trillion. Crédit Agricole says 6% real GDP growth with 5% interest rates would be needed just to stabilise debt.

Crédit Agricole's rates strategist sees gridlock as mildly bullish for the long end, since fewer spending programs and tax cuts ease term premium and flatten the curve. The front end stays high because energy prices are elevated and the Fed is likely to deliver more hikes. Crédit Agricole forecasts the 10Y at 5.05% at year-end and 5.10% in March, against 5.01% in JPM's morning print.

The FOMC held at 3.75%-4.00% as expected, with two hawkish dissents from Hammack and Lisa Cook. JPM's Feroli had expected Logan, not Cook, to dissent alongside Hammack. JPM economists still expect one more hike in December and then a hold.

Crédit Agricole's study of every US election since 1976 finds the dollar weakened after a Democratic Congress with a GOP president. It rallied when a GOP president and Senate faced a Democratic House, as after the 2018 midterms, which coincided with a recovering economy and a hawkish Fed. The dollar-weak episodes also featured a slowing economy, Fed cuts and a Middle East conflict.

Crédit Agricole's base case is a cooling AI capex boom, gridlock and fading fiscal support, then Fed cuts in H2 2027. It forecasts EUR/USD rising from 1.13 at year-end to 1.17 by December 2027, and USD/JPY falling from 156 to 150.

Crédit Agricole forecasts gold at $5,000 by year-end and $5,500 by end-2027, against $4,051 in JPM's Wednesday print. Gold gained roughly 2% in the month after past government shutdowns, and a shutdown next year is a decent chance.

The World Gold Council says elections have had no consistent or significant effect on gold. In 2016 and 2024 gold fell initially on Trump's win and then recovered much of the move. The WGC argues a Democratic Congress is gold-supportive through limits on war funding, tighter AI regulation and wider executive and emergency powers. It expects non-US buyers to keep bidding even if Republicans win.

On Iran, Crédit Agricole's EM head sees no clear-cut conclusion for EMs from a shift left, because it depends on Trump's assertiveness. Less leeway could mean less pressure on Iran or more assertiveness. The WSJ reported on Tuesday night that Washington told Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the midterms. Brent briefly topped $116.50 before Tehran's foreign minister said it was still giving diplomacy a chance.

Deutsche Bank's Chadha and Thatte find the S&P was higher in the three months from early October in 21 of the last 23 midterm years. The S&P typically slides 4-5% into an early-October trough. 2026 has been a gentler version: a record on May 29, up about 11% YTD, and less than 1% higher five months later.

JPM's desk remains Tactically Bullish, citing about 30% Q3 EPS growth and sentiment stuck in Extreme Fear. It concedes there has been no complete positioning washout. Its main risk is a Middle East escalation that targets energy infrastructure.

JPM factor specialist Manish Sinha notes junk has been rallying while Quality was down 2 sigma at one point. He reads the market as pricing a dovish Fed, resolution of geopolitical conflicts and a renewed AI capex upcycle without funding needs, and calls that a low-probability combination.

The author sides with Sinha. Over the past 24 hours the Fed delivered two hawkish dissents, Alphabet fell 10% after hours on AI-capex doubts, and a military campaign was reportedly planned for the week after the vote. The author argues seasonality and gridlock say little about $116 Brent or a 5% 10Y, and that a Democratic win could be the catalyst for a correction.

tension_points.bull_case: Deutsche Bank finds the S&P rose in the three months from early October in 21 of the last 23 midterm years. JPM's desk is Tactically Bullish on about 30% Q3 EPS growth and Extreme Fear sentiment. Gridlock is seen as market friendly.
tension_points.bear_case: JPM's Sinha says the market is pricing a dovish Fed, geopolitical resolution and a renewed AI capex upcycle at once, which is a low-probability combination. The Fed just delivered two hawkish dissents, Brent is above $116, the 10Y is near 5% and Alphabet fell 10% after hours.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An escalation in the Middle East that targets energy infrastructure, which JPM names as the main risk to its bullish view.

tension_points.bull_case: When a GOP president and Senate faced a Democratic House, as after 2018, the dollar rallied across the board, helped by a recovering economy and a hawkish Fed.
tension_points.bear_case: With a GOP president and a Democratic Congress, the dollar weakened in the months after the vote. Crédit Agricole's base case adds a cooling AI capex boom, fading fiscal support and Fed cuts in H2 2027.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The weaker-dollar episodes also featured a slowing economy, Fed rate cuts and a Middle East conflict. Only the conflict is present today, so the dollar-weak case needs the other two to appear.

tension_points.bull_case: Less presidential leeway under a Democratic Congress could mean less pressure on Iran, and Tehran says it is still giving diplomacy a chance.
tension_points.bear_case: Trump could act more assertively to offset lost leeway, and the WSJ reported the Pentagon told Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the vote.
